newsitem.title: SPAIN: Mexico says keen to issue more debt to prepay IMF.
newsitem.headline: Mexico says keen to issue more debt to prepay IMF.

text.p: Mexico will make further prepayments to the International Monetary Fund following its crisis bail-out package if market conditions allow it to issue more international long-term debt, Mexico's deputy finance minister Martin Werner said.
The United States threw together a $20 billion package and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) added $17.8 billion to rescue the Mexican economy after a shock peso devaluation in December 1994.
Mexico only drew down $12.5 billion from the United States and has already paid it back in full.
In January Mexico said it owed the IMF $11.6 billion and by early March it had prepaid $3.1 billion.

"We've paid the IMF already $800 million over the last two months. We continue to be successful in replacing long-term debt and we will probably make further repayments to the IMF," Werner said in an interview on the edges of the Inter-American Development Bank's 38th annual meeting.
Further repayments would depend on market conditions.
"If there's a lot of liquidity in world capital markets and we can place long-term debt, we can make some further repayments to the Fund," he said.
Werner said Mexico would be most interested in issuing fresh debt with a maturity of around 10 years.
"The 10-year benchmark is fine -- with between five- and 10-year tenor debt we can make further repayments," he said. "We could consider payments in many currencies, not just U.S. dollars."
"There is no rush to repay the debt but if there's a lot of liquidity in the markets we will do it," he said.
He also said Mexico's rate of domestic consumption, which plummeted when the country plunged into recession in 1995, was starting to improve.

"Consumption is picking up. In fact in 1996 private consumption grew by 2.3 percent, less than GDP which grew 5.1 percent, but it's definitely picking up," he said in an interview broadcast on Reuters Financial Television.
"We are seeing that the sector's link to internal demand is recovering but it will grow by less than output," he added.
"We're seeing inflation coming down in February, and in March and April significantly," he said, but declined to give any forecasts for the coming months. -- Barcelona newsroom +34 3 424 2659
